## Course objectives

This course provides the tools needed to carry out empirical research in social and political sciences, and to develop a high-quality research project for the BA Thesis. The course combines the critical reading of empirical research articles, identifying their strengths and weaknesses, with the practice of writing one: a clear research question, a literature review with a theoretical argument, a research design section describing the case, data, and method, and a results section that precedes a discussion/conclusion. Its specific focus is on mastering the description and execution of that research design, building on prior quantitative and qualitative training to map sources, designs, and methods onto research questions in political science. Along the way, students strengthen the general competencies expected of any researcher: working effectively in a group, communicating ideas clearly in both oral and written form, organizing and planning research individually and collectively, handling complex information in a structured way, and understanding existing theory well enough to identify the main positions in an academic debate and the empirical evidence used to support each of them.

At the level of specific skills, students will learn to formulate a research problem or question; to develop the concepts and typologies needed to analyze a specific research topic; to theorize, building an argument that addresses that problem on its own terms; and to derive testable hypotheses from that theory. They will practice finding data and defining measures suited to a given research question, and identifying, organizing, and analyzing information critically and systematically. The course also develops the capacity to identify appropriate methods for analyzing data and measurement, combining knowledge of quantitative and qualitative techniques with the judgment to choose which is best suited to a given problem in the social sciences, including a first introduction to R.

By the end of the course, students will be able to test hypotheses against evidence and to reason explicitly about the relationship between theory, method, and the broader aims of a research project, the same three-part logic (motivation and theory, qualitative design, quantitative design) that structures the mixed-method group project developed throughout the semester.

## Course structure

The course runs in two weekly tracks that are taught in parallel but do not always meet in the same week given the structure of (local and national) bank holidays. Three Mondays fall on public holidays (Oct 12, Nov 2, Dec 7), so those weeks have a lecture only and no seminar.

- **Lectures (MAG, Fridays)**: 14 sessions covering research design and quantitative methods, from the logic of scientific inquiry to difference-in-differences designs, including the introduction of R software, its logic and packages.
- **Reduced seminars (RED, Mondays)**: 11 sessions combining critical discussion of assigned readings, presentation of group work, and applied practice in R.

## Evaluation

| Component | Weight |
|---|---|
| Final written exam | 40% |
| Group paper critical presentation in seminar session | 10% |
| Three critical questions in seminars | 10% |
| Group project I: Motivation, research question, literature review, hypotheses (~1,500 words) | 10% |
| Group project II: Presentation of a qualitative design, data, and refinement (~2,500 words) | 15% |
| Group project III: quantitative design, discussion of causal identification beyond OLS, preliminary analyses (~4,000 words) | 15% |

Groups are formed in the first seminar (Sept 7), group presentations will be set that date. A minimum grade of 3.5/10 on the exam is required to pass the course.

1. **Final written exam.** Friday 18/12/2026. Multiple option questions and short hand writing tasks. The exam will be conducted in class and without computers.
2. **Group paper critical presentation.** Each group will present and critically evaluate an article in the syllabus (assigned for the week). 15' presentation.
3. **Three critical questions.** Each student will have to throw at least three critically informed questions about the papers and the content of the seminar sessions.
4. **Group project.** Each group will develop a short research paper throughout the course, in three steps:

| Step | Content | Presentation date | Manuscript due |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Motivation, question, brief argument based on previous literature | Sept 28 | Oct 1 |
| 2 | Fix mistakes, qual design, brief data collection and analysis (qual) | Oct 26 | Oct 29 |
| 3 | Fix mistakes, quant design, data collection, analysis, interpretation | Nov 23 | Nov 26 |

### Use of AI

Artificial intelligence tools (ChatGPT, Claude, and similar) are powerful aids for this course, but only when used with control, moderation, and human supervision. Students remain fully responsible for the accuracy, originality, and quality of everything they submit. Any hallucinated citations or evidence, or any form of plagiarism (AI-generated or otherwise), will be evaluated with a grade of zero.

## Weekly schedule

### Lectures (MAG), Fridays, 12:30–14:00

**L1 (Sept 11). Course presentation and introduction to empirical research in social and political science.** Group formation for the course's project and the reduced session activities.

- Schwartz, M. A. (2008). The importance of stupidity in scientific research. *Journal of Cell Science*, 121(11), 1771–1771.
- Kellstedt & Whitten (2018), *The Fundamentals of Political Science Research*, Ch. 1.

**L2 (Sept 18). The research process I: from the question to hypotheses.**

- Nussio, E. (2024). The "Dark Side" of Community Ties: Collective Action and Lynching in Mexico. *American Sociological Review*, 00031224241253268.
- Baglione (2016), *Writing a Research Paper in Political Science*, Ch. 2.
- Extra ball: [Cyrus Samii's blog](https://cyrussamii.com/?p=3682); Kalyvas, S. N. (2006). *The Logic of Violence in Civil War*. Cambridge University Press. Ch 7: A theory of selective violence (p. 173–210).

**L3 (Sept 25). The research process II: from shoe-leather to experimental approaches.**

- [Harvard Online video about John Snow](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lNjrAXGRda4)

- Treisman, D. (2020). Democracy by mistake: How the errors of autocrats trigger transitions to freer government. *American Political Science Review*, 114(3), 792–810.

- Dunning, T., et al. (2019). Voter information campaigns and political accountability: Cumulative findings from a preregistered meta-analysis of coordinated trials. *Science Advances*, 5(7), eaaw2612.

**L4 (Oct 2). Counterfactuals and measurement. Intro to R.**

- Fearon, J. D. (1991). Counterfactuals and hypothesis testing in political science. *World Politics*, 43(2), 169–195.

- Pager, D., & Quillian, L. (2005). Walking the talk? What employers say versus what they do. *American Sociological Review*, 70(3), 355–380.

**L5 (Oct 9). Qualitative methods I: Case studies, in-depth interviews, and focus groups.**

- Giusti-Rodríguez, M. (2024). From Social Networks to Political Parties: Indigenous Party-Building in Bolivia. *American Political Science Review*, 118(4), 1803–1823.
- Academic presentation by [Álvaro Canalejo-Molero](https://acanalejo.github.io/) (CSIC): Two ways of using focus groups.

**L6 (Oct 16). T-test, p-value, OLS.**

- Gerber, A. and Green, D. (2000). The effect of a nonpartisan get-out-the-vote drive: an experimental study of leafletting. *Journal of Politics*, vol. 62.
- Angrist, J. D., & Pischke, J. S. (2014). *Mastering'metrics: The Path from Cause to Effect*. Princeton University Press. Introduction: p. XI–XV; Ch 2, Section 1: p. 47–55.

**L7 (Oct 23). Multivariate regression. Regression with R.**

- Fearon, J. D., & Laitin, D. D. (2003). Ethnicity, Insurgency, and Civil War. *American Political Science Review*, 97(1), 75–90. [Replication analysis]
- Bolet, D. (2021). Drinking alone: local socio-cultural degradation and radical right support. *Comparative Political Studies*, 54(9), 1653–1692.

**L8 (Oct 30). Why? How? Qualitative methods II: Ethnography and process tracing.**

- Berenschot, W. (2010). Everyday mediation: The politics of public service delivery in Gujarat, India. *Development and Change*, 41(5), 883–905.
- Pavone, T., & Stiansen, Ø. (2022). The shadow effect of courts: Judicial review and the politics of preemptive reform. *American Political Science Review*, 116(1), 322–336.

**L9 (Nov 6). Experiments: The golden standard.**

- Prillaman, S. A. (2023). Strength in numbers: how women's groups close India's political gender gap. *American Journal of Political Science*, 67(2), 390–410.
- Clayton, A., O'Brien, D. Z., & Piscopo, J. M. (2019). All male panels? Representation and democratic legitimacy. *American Journal of Political Science*, 63(1), 113–129.
- Extra ball: Mousa, S. (2020). Building social cohesion between Christians and Muslims through soccer in post-ISIS Iraq. *Science*, 369(6505), 866–870.

**L10 (Nov 13). Difference-in-Differences.**

- Angrist, J. D., & Pischke, J. S. (2014). *Mastering'metrics*. Ch. 5, Parallel worlds.
- Montalvo, J. G. (2011). Voting after the bombings. *Review of Economics and Statistics*, 93(4), 1146–1154.

**L11 (Nov 20). Regression discontinuity design.**

- Angrist, J. D., & Pischke, J. S. (2014). *Mastering'metrics*. Ch. 6, Getting a little jumpy.
- Dinas, E., Riera, P., & Roussias, N. (2015). Staying in the first league. *Political Science Research and Methods*, 3(2), 187–204.

**L12 (Nov 27). Instrumental variables.**

- Angrist, J. D., & Pischke, J. S. (2014). *Mastering'metrics*. Ch. 4, Instrumental Variables in Action.
- Hangartner, D., Dinas, E., Marbach, M., Matakos, K., & Xefteris, D. (2019). Does exposure to the refugee crisis make natives more hostile? *American Political Science Review*, 113(2), 442–455.
- Dell, M. and Querubín, P. (2018). Nation building through foreign intervention: evidence from discontinuities in military strategies. *The Quarterly Journal of Economics*.

**L13 (Dec 4). Mixed-methods and outside the box: The real gold standard.**

- Bos, A. L., Greenlee, J. S., Holman, M. R., Oxley, Z. M., & Lay, J. C. (2022). This one's for the boys: How gendered political socialization limits girls' political ambition and interest. *American Political Science Review*, 116(2), 484–501.
- Lake, M., & Hartman, A. C. (2025). Institutions as perpetrators: Power and political violence in responses to rape. *Perspectives on Politics*, 1–22.

**L14 (Dec 11, last day of classes). More presentations and wrap-up.** No readings assigned.

### Seminars (RED), Mondays, 12:30–14:00

**S0 (Sept 7). Cancelled.**

**S1 (Sept 14). Plagiarism, fishing, and the limits of applying the scientific method** as used in the natural sciences, to social reality.

- Don Green – LaCour issue: two press articles
- Broockman, D., & Kalla, J. (2016). Durably reducing transphobia: A field experiment on door-to-door canvassing. *Science*, 352(6282), 220–224.

**S2 (Sept 21). Motivation and research questions.** Read Samii's blog and article. Identify three societal problems; we will comment on how to turn that into research questions and motivate them for a broader audience.

- Baglione, Ch. 4.
- [Cyrus Samii's blog](https://cyrussamii.com/?p=3682)
- Samii, C. (2023). Methodologies for "Political Science as Problem Solving". In *Oxford Handbook of Engaged Methodological Pluralism in Political Science*. Oxford University Press.
- Read the introduction of: Bush, S. S., & Clayton, A. (2023). Facing change: Gender and climate change attitudes worldwide. *American Political Science Review*, 117(2), 591–608.

**S3 (Sept 28). Literature review vs. theory sections.** This session will help write helpful literature reviews, building hypotheses that theoretically answer our research questions. 5–10' presentation of the first part of the project.

- Read Lit and Theory sections: Goyal, T. (2023). Representation from below: How women's grassroots party activism promotes equal political participation. *American Political Science Review*, 1–16.
- Read Intro, Concepts, Lit, Theory: Juon, A. (2025). The long-term consequences of power-sharing for ethnic salience. *Journal of Peace Research*, 62(3), 613–628.

**S4 (Oct 5). Intro to R: Tidyverse and ggplot.** 

- [Introduction to R and Tidyverse](https://jhudatascience.org/tidyversecourse/intro.html)
- [ggplot2-book.org/introduction](https://ggplot2-book.org/introduction)
- [ggplot2-book.org/getting-started](https://ggplot2-book.org/getting-started)

**S5 (Oct 19). Qualitative methods: case studies.**

- Lapuente, V., & Rothstein, B. (2014). Civil war Spain versus Swedish harmony: the quality of government factor. *Comparative Political Studies*, 47(10), 1416–1441.

**S6 (Oct 26). Qualitative methods: interview and process tracing.** 5–10' presentation of the second part of the project.

- Kantola, J., & Lombardo, E. (2019). Populism and feminist politics: The cases of Finland and Spain. *European Journal of Political Research*, 58(4), 1108–1128.

- Pavone, T., & Stiansen, Ø. (2022). The shadow effect of courts. *American Political Science Review*, 116(1), 322–336.

**S7 (Nov 9). Introduction to R (II): OLS and selection problems.** Discussion: how would a regression answer your research question?

- Kitschelt, H., & Rehm, P. (2014). Occupations as a site of political preference formation. *Comparative Political Studies*, 47(12), 1670–1706.
- Fearon, J. D., & Laitin, D. D. (2003). Ethnicity, Insurgency, and Civil War. *American Political Science Review*, 97(1), 75–90. [Replication analysis]

**S8 (Nov 16). Experiments: What's the experiment that fits your research question? Intro to natural experiments.**

- Cilliers, J., Dube, O., & Siddiqi, B. (2016). Reconciling after civil conflict increases social capital but decreases individual well-being. *Science*, 352(6287), 787–794.
- Croke, K., Grossman, G., Larreguy, H. A., & Marshall, J. (2016). Deliberate disengagement: How education can decrease political participation in electoral authoritarian regimes. *American Political Science Review*, 110(3), 579–600.

**S9 (Nov 23). Seminar (I): Final group project presentations and discussions.**

**S10 (Nov 30). Seminar (II): Final group project presentations and discussions.** Final manuscript submission: Dec 2.
